key_terms.meaning: A material with at least one dimension between about 1 nm and 100 nm (1 nm = 10⁻⁹ m), so that surface and quantum effects dominate its behaviour.
Surface area divided by volume; it rises as 1/r for a particle of radius r, so a 10 nm particle has far more exposed atoms than a 10 μm one.
Restricting an electron to a box smaller than its natural wavelength, which pushes its energy levels apart and raises the band gap.
Making nanostructures by cutting, milling or etching bulk material down to nanometre size.
Making nanostructures by assembling atoms, ions or molecules into larger ordered structures.
A bottom-up route where a metal alkoxide or salt forms a colloidal sol, then a gel, which is dried and calcined to a nano-oxide powder.
A semiconductor crystal 2–10 nm across in all three directions, whose colour is set by its size through quantum confinement.
A rolled graphene sheet forming a hollow cylinder a few nm wide; it can be single-walled (SWCNT) or multi-walled (MWCNT).
The energy difference between the top of the valence band and the bottom of the conduction band in a solid, measured in electron volts (eV).
Adding a tiny amount of impurity (ppm level) to a semiconductor to raise the electron count (n-type) or the hole count (p-type).
The energy up to which states are filled at 0 K; doping shifts it towards the conduction band (n-type) or valence band (p-type).
Alignment of atomic magnetic moments in the same direction below the Curie temperature, giving a large permanent magnetisation.
The temperature above which a ferromagnet loses its spontaneous magnetisation and becomes paramagnetic.
Complete expulsion of magnetic field lines from the interior of a superconductor when it is cooled below its critical temperature.
The temperature at which a material's electrical resistance drops abruptly to zero.
A liquid crystal whose phase changes are produced by changing temperature alone.
A liquid crystal whose phases appear when a solvent concentration is changed, as in soap-water systems.
A liquid-crystal phase with parallel molecular orientation but no positional order; the director n marks the average direction.
Thin-film growth in which a solid source is evaporated or sputtered in vacuum and condenses on the substrate.
Thin-film growth in which gaseous precursors react on a heated substrate surface to deposit a solid film.

takeaways: Below about 100 nm the fraction of atoms sitting on the surface becomes large, and behaviour changes from bulk-like to size-controlled.
Quantum confinement raises the band gap as a crystal shrinks, which is why quantum dot colour depends on particle size.
Nanomaterials are made either by breaking bulk matter down (top-down) or by building up from atoms (bottom-up); each direction has its own defects and cost profile.
Band structure, not chemistry alone, decides whether a solid conducts like a metal, insulates, or semiconducts.
Doping shifts the Fermi level and changes carrier type, and it is the basis of every diode, transistor and solar cell.
Superconductors carry current with zero resistance and expel magnetic field; both effects end above a critical temperature.
Magnetic order disappears above the Curie temperature, so magnet choice is always a temperature decision.
Liquid crystals keep orientational order while flowing, and a small applied voltage can rotate that order — the basis of LCDs.
PVD gives controlled, dense films but poor step coverage; CVD gives conformal coatings but needs volatile precursors and higher substrate temperature.
bank_note: Long answers are usually asked as compare-and-contrast or explain-with-examples questions, so give the definition, the physical reason, one worked example with numbers or units, and two or three named applications.

bank.q: Classify nanomaterials on the basis of dimensionality and give one example of each class.
outline: 0-D: quantum dots, nanoparticles — confined in all three directions
1-D: nanotubes, nanowires, nanorods — confined in two
2-D: thin films, graphene, layered clays — confined in one
3-D: bulk nanocomposites built from the above
State that at least one dimension lies between 1 and 100 nm

bank.q: Explain why surface area and quantum confinement make a nanomaterial behave differently from the same bulk solid.
outline: Surface-to-volume ratio scales as 1/r; worked example with 10 nm vs 10 μm particles
Consequence: higher reactivity, lower melting point, better catalysis and adsorption
Quantum confinement: electron confined in a box smaller than its de Broglie wavelength
Energy levels become discrete and the gap widens; band gap scales roughly as 1/d² for a particle of diameter d
Resulting changes in colour, band gap and conductivity

bank.q: Compare top-down and bottom-up approaches to nanomaterial synthesis, with two examples of each.
outline: Top-down: start from bulk, remove material — ball milling, lithography, etching
Bottom-up: start from atoms/molecules, assemble — sol-gel, CVD, molecular beam epitaxy
Compare on defect density, purity, cost, throughput and size control
State which direction suits which product

bank.q: Draw and explain the band structure of a metal, an insulator and a semiconductor, and show how doping changes the Fermi level.
outline: Band gap E_g: zero or overlapping bands for a metal, roughly 1 eV or less for a semiconductor, above about 4 eV for an insulator
Fermi level position in each case
n-type donor level just below conduction band; E_F moves up
p-type acceptor level just above valence band; E_F moves down
Conductivity rises with doping; mention the mass-action relation n·p = constant at fixed temperature

bank.q: Distinguish thermotropic and lyotropic liquid crystals and describe nematic, smectic and cholesteric phases.
outline: Thermotropic: phase transitions driven by temperature, mesogen is pure compound
Lyotropic: driven by solvent concentration and amphiphile structure
Nematic: parallel orientation, no positional order
Smectic: layered positional order in addition to orientation
Cholesteric (twisted nematic): director rotates in a helical pitch; strongly optically active
One example of each class

bank.q: Compare PVD and CVD techniques for thin-film formation, listing advantages, limitations and uses.
outline: PVD: evaporation and sputtering, vacuum, physical transfer of atoms
CVD: gaseous precursors react on a heated substrate
PVD gives good thickness control and purity but poor step coverage
CVD gives conformal coating over complex shapes but needs volatile precursors and higher temperature
Uses: metallisation and optical coatings for PVD; polysilicon, silicon nitride and hard coatings for CVD

bank.q: The colour of a cadmium selenide quantum dot changes from blue to red as the crystal grows. Explain this with quantum confinement and estimate the trend in band gap.
outline: Particle-in-a-box energy spacing rises as size falls
Effective band gap = bulk band gap + confinement term proportional to 1/d²
Small dot: larger gap, blue-shifted absorption and emission
Large dot: smaller gap, red-shifted emission
Exciton Bohr radius sets the size range where this matters
Applications: displays, bioimaging labels, solar cells

bank.q: Describe the sol-gel preparation of zinc oxide and titanium dioxide nanostructures and explain how pH, precursor and calcination temperature change the product.
outline: Precursor choice: zinc acetate or zinc nitrate; titanium isopropoxide or titanium tetrachloride
Hydrolysis and condensation to sol, then gel network
pH controls hydrolysis rate and particle size; base usually gives finer particles
Drying and calcination convert hydroxide to oxide and set crystallite size; higher temperature sinters and grows particles
Characterisation by XRD for crystallite size and UV-Vis for band gap
Properties and uses: photocatalytic TiO2, UV-blocking ZnO, gas sensing

bank.q: Explain how a twisted nematic liquid crystal display switches a pixel on and off.
outline: Nematic liquid crystal with positive dielectric anisotropy, aligned by rubbed polyimide
Polariser and analyser crossed; 90° twisted structure rotates light so the cell is bright with no voltage
Applied voltage aligns molecules along the field and destroys the twist, so light is blocked
Threshold and saturation voltages; response time in milliseconds
Colour filters and backlight make a colour pixel; mention viewing-angle and temperature limits

bank.q: You must coat a deep narrow trench uniformly with a thin nitride film. Choose PVD or CVD and justify the choice.
outline: Line-of-sight deposition in PVD gives shadowing and poor step coverage
CVD reactants diffuse to surfaces and react, giving conformal coverage
Need volatile, thermally stable precursors and a suitable substrate temperature
Compare film stress, deposition rate, and process cost
Mention plasma-enhanced CVD as a lower-temperature variant

bank.q: Explain superconductivity, the Meissner effect, and the difference between Type I and Type II superconductors, with applications.
outline: Zero resistance below critical temperature T_c; perfect diamagnetism (Meissner effect) is a separate property
Type I: single critical field, complete flux expulsion, soft superconductors
Type II: two critical fields, flux penetrates as vortices between them, higher T_c, hard superconductors
Applications: MRI magnets, maglev, power cables, SQUID sensors
Limits: cryogenic cooling cost and mechanical brittleness of ceramic superconductors

bank.q: Compare carbon nanotubes and quantum dots as materials for display and bio-imaging applications, weighing performance against safety and cost.
outline: CNT: high aspect ratio, ballistic conduction, mechanical strength, but chirality control is hard and there are asbestos-like toxicity concerns for long fibres
Quantum dots: tunable narrow emission, high brightness, but often contain cadmium or lead, raising heavy-metal toxicity questions
Compare on quantum yield, photostability, dispersibility and functionalisation
Cost and scale-up issues
Suggest encapsulation or non-toxic alternatives and state a reasoned verdict

bank.q: Compare top-down and bottom-up routes for industrial-scale nanomaterial production, judging cost, purity, defect density and reproducibility.
outline: Top-down: high throughput, cheap, but introduces surface damage, broad size distribution and contamination from the milling medium
Bottom-up: better size and shape control, higher purity, but slower, uses expensive precursors and needs careful process control
Defect density and crystallinity comparison
Reproducibility and batch-to-batch variation
Link the final choice to the application, for example catalyst versus drug carrier
Environmental and worker-safety factors in both routes

bank.q: Explain magnetic materials by classifying them as diamagnetic, paramagnetic, ferromagnetic and ferrimagnetic, and relate the Fermi level and band picture to their use in devices.
outline: Origin of atomic magnetic moment: spin and orbital motion of electrons
Diamagnetic, paramagnetic, ferromagnetic, antiferromagnetic and ferrimagnetic behaviour
Domains, hysteresis, soft versus hard magnets with B-H loop interpretation
Curie temperature and loss of order on heating
Device choice: soft iron for transformer cores, hard ferrites for permanent magnets
Magnetic storage and spintronics as advanced applications

glossary.def: A particle with all three dimensions between about 1 nm and 100 nm.
A one-dimensional nanostructure that is nanometre-wide but much longer in one direction.
A single sheet of carbon atoms one atom thick, arranged in a hexagonal lattice.
A semiconductor nanocrystal small enough in all three directions to show size-tunable, discrete energy levels.
A seamless cylindrical roll of graphene, either single-walled or multi-walled.
The energy gap between the top of the valence band and the bottom of the conduction band.
The highest filled band of energy levels in a solid at 0 K.
The lowest empty band in a solid through which electrons can carry current.
The energy level with a 50 per cent occupation probability at thermal equilibrium.
A semiconductor doped with a donor impurity, so that electrons are the majority carriers.
A semiconductor doped with an acceptor impurity, so that holes are the majority carriers.
Weak magnetisation opposite to the applied field, shown by all materials but often masked.
Weak magnetisation in the same direction as the applied field, with no order once the field is removed.
Antiparallel alignment of unequal magnetic moments, giving a net spontaneous magnetisation.
The B-H loop traced when a magnetic field is cycled; its area is energy lost per cycle.
The state below a critical temperature in which electrical resistance is exactly zero.
Complete expulsion of magnetic flux from a superconductor cooled below its critical temperature.
A superconductor that admits magnetic flux as vortices between two critical fields, allowing higher operating fields.
A molecule that can form a liquid-crystalline phase because of its rigid rod or disc shape.
A unit vector describing the average molecular orientation in a liquid-crystal phase.
A liquid-crystal phase with molecules arranged in layers as well as aligned.
A twisted nematic arrangement in which the director rotates in a helix with a characteristic pitch.
A layer of material from a few nanometres to a few micrometres thick on a substrate.
A PVD process in which energetic ions knock atoms off a target, which then deposit on the substrate.
